extracted.intended_audience: NSF principal investigators and academic researchers preparing NSF proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for preparing, submitting, and (if declined) revising National Science Foundation research proposals, including how funded PIs differ and how to respond to panel feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak or Missing Broader Impacts — Many PIs treat the broader impacts section as an afterthought; NSF reviewers score broader impacts as a co-equal criterion with intellectual merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate broader impacts into the research design rather than bolting them on as a separate section. Example: build analysis tools as open-source packages with documentation and tutorials for community college instructors. A proposal with outstanding science and generic broader impacts will lose to one with strong science and genuinely thoughtful broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Merit (co-equal with Broader Impacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual merit is scored as a co-equal criterion with broader impacts and must be addressed clearly in the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the scientific significance, novelty, and potential to advance knowledge are explicit and balanced with the broader impacts plan; reviewers compare both criteria when ranking proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Plan: clarity, scope, and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Unclear or Overly Ambitious Research Plan — Reviewers must believe the project is both important and feasible within the proposed timeline and budget; the common failure mode is trying to do too much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope ruthlessly. Prefer three well-defined aims with clear milestones over five ambitious aims. Make sure methods match the aims and the timeline/budget. Avoid spreading work so thin that feasibility is doubtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Aims, Deliverables, and Milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Each aim should have a concrete deliverable, a clear methodology, and an explanation of what happens if a particular approach does not work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe deliverables and milestones explicitly; reviewers favor concrete, testable objectives. Tie each piece of the plan to measurable outputs and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency Planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers want to see that you have thought about contingencies, not just the optimistic path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each aim/method, state alternative approaches, decision points, and how failures will be handled so reviewers are confident the project can still produce valuable outcomes if initial approaches fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary Data: adequacy and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Insufficient Preliminary Data — NSF does not expect completed research, but reviewers need evidence that the approach is feasible. The gap is often about how preliminary data are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a single well-designed pilot with clear results and honest discussion of limitations over many uninterpreted figures. Connect every piece of preliminary data to a specific aim; explain why the pilot supports the proposed approach if methods differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with Program Solicitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor Alignment with the Program Solicitation — Each NSF program has specific priorities; proposals that do not address those priorities will be declined regardless of scientific quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the program officer before submitting (a brief conversation can confirm fit and current priorities). Tailor the proposal to the solicitation's stated priorities and language; do not assume a strong proposal from another context will fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and communication for a broad/interdisciplinary panel
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing That Does Not Communicate to a Broad Panel — NSF panels are interdisciplinary; proposals that assume too much domain knowledge will score poorly on clarity even if the science is excellent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make arguments accessible without dumbing down. Have someone outside your immediate subfield read the proposal; if they cannot explain the main idea in two sentences, revise for clarity. Avoid excessive jargon and define specialized terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget and administrative compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Budget or Administrative Issues — Common problems include budgets that do not match the scope of work, missing required sections (data management plan, mentoring plan for postdocs), and page limit violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a systematic checklist against the current NSF Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG). Ensure budgets match scope, include all required sections, respect page limits, and follow institutional/agency rules to avoid avoidable rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and analyze the panel summary like a reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: After rejection, the panel summary synthesizes reviewers' views and is the most valuable document you will receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wait a few days, then read with a pen and mark every specific critique. Categorize critiques as 'Fixable in revision' (unclear writing, missing preliminary data, budget justification), 'Requires rethinking' (scope too broad, wrong program fit, fundamental methodology concerns), or 'Disagreements' (places reviewer misunderstood the proposal). Use this categorization to plan next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to the program officer (debrief) after rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: You can and should request a debrief with the program officer after every declined proposal; they provide context not in the written reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask how the panel ranked the proposal relative to others, whether concerns were unanimous or split, and whether a resubmission is worthwhile. Some POs will tell you directly if resubmitting to the same program makes sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to resubmit, pivot, or split the project
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every rejected proposal should be resubmitted to the same program; choice depends on whether issues are addressable or fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reviews show addressable concerns, resubmit (NSF does not penalize resubmissions). If concerns are fundamental or about fit, consider submitting to a different NSF program, reframing for another agency (NIH, DOE, DOD), or splitting an overly ambitious proposal into two focused proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen the proposal systematically for resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: When resubmitting, do not just patch specific issues; reassess and strengthen the entire proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite the project summary and broader impacts from scratch, ask at least two colleagues outside your subfield to review the revised draft, verify alignment with any new program priorities, and update preliminary data with any new results. Demonstrate responsiveness to feedback rather than superficial edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use checklists and keep current with PAPPG changes
rubrics_metrics.description: PAPPG changes regularly and requirements that applied to a prior submission may have changed; administrative oversights are an avoidable cause of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and use a current submission checklist tied to the most recent PAPPG. Check for required documents (data management plan, mentoring plan), institutional forms, and formatting/page limits before finalizing submission.
